A friend of mine owns a helicopter business, a few weeks ago he needed to go to another city on business and invited me with him. The other city was about an hours flight away and mostly the flight was over water. On the way back he asked me if I wanted to fly the helicopter. I said, "um, yeah".

The chopper was a Bell 407, not huge, but not tiny either. It fits 7 people. I was sitting in the co-pilots seat and my pedals were disconnected, but my pilot friend said they really weren't that important anyway. The helicopter has a stick for flying and a bar that you raise and twist for propeller speed. He set that bar and for most of the trip it was not touched, he didn't even really explain to me how it worked. The only thing I manipulated was the stick.

Now you may think, "Yawn, whatever, the pilot probably did a lot of behind the scenes work while OP pretended to fly". I shit you not, every time I looked over at him he was either texting or staring off to the side.

Now, the stick was really weird. I will try to explain it to you guys.

  • If you push it forward, the helicopter goes into a nose dive and loses altitude while gaining speed.

  • If you push it back, the helicopter starts climbing and speed is decreased.

  • if you push it left or right the entire chopper tilts left or right, respectively.

  • if you move the stick diagonally between left and forward it simply turns left...like a car.

  • I honestly didn't quite figure out what tilting it back diagonally did...you have to understand, most of time I was on the verge of shitting my pants out of fear.

The stick is EXTREMELY sensitive. None of this game style pushing the joystick all the way to the left nonsense. Most of my movements could have been measured in millimeters. Movements through turbulence could be measured in 1-2 centimeters.

Now, the flying itself wasn't all that hard actually, what was difficult was maintaining a comfortable flight and staying within parameters, ie., altitude, direction of travel, and speed. Remember, you want to stay at a certain speed, but if a gust of wind hits you and you have to push back to adjust your altitude you end up losing speed as well. On top of all of that, the entire time, the helicopter wants to kill you because you are laughing in the face of aerodynamics. I swear to god, there were times where I was flying, there was no wind or turbulence, and suddenly the damn thing starts banking left. When I told the pilot, he simply replied, "Yup, the helicopter is going to do what it wants to do, your job is just to keep it from crashing."

O.O "uhh ok"

After about 40 minutes of flight we approached the airport and he let me do the final approach and an attempt at landing. It's kinda weird, on approach we had to actually line up with the runway and follow it, as if we were landing a real airplane. Ultimately, the whole flying, and even approach, wasn't too bad. I picked it up immediately and can honestly say that, in a pinch, I would be able to fly a helicopter again. Landing though. Fuck landing.

Once we flew down the runway and approached the helicopter landing sites he asked me if I wanted to try to land. "Uhhh I don't know about that"

He just replied, "It's a little tricky, I'll put us in a hover and you try to maintain it while I set us down, It will feel like balancing on a ball bearing"

"uhhh, seriously...think----"

"Ok, See? You're hovering now! Just try to keep it level"

He was joking about it feeling like you were trying to balance on a ball bearing of course, It was more akin to trying to balance an elephant with a temper tantrum on a ball that's in turn on a boat in a raging storm. I probably kept it in hover for all of one second, then the helicopter started thrashing around every which possible way and no movement of the stick was doing anything noticeable.

"Pilot! PILOT! DUDE! I REALLY THINK YOU SHOULD TAKE OVER!!!"

He started laughing and leveled it out in an instant, then the fucker, i shit you not, flew forward to a different landing spot and parallel parked the damn thing like this.

One of the best days of my life.
